questions.question: Which six Functions organize cybersecurity outcomes at the highest level of the CSF Core?
questions.answer: The six CSF Core Functions are GOVERN, IDENTIFY, PROTECT, DETECT, RESPOND, and RECOVER.
acceptable_answers: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.

claims.text: GOVERN is a CSF Core Function.
IDENTIFY is a CSF Core Function.
PROTECT is a CSF Core Function.
DETECT is a CSF Core Function.
RESPOND is a CSF Core Function.
RECOVER is a CSF Core Function.

evidence.text: The CSF Core Functions — GOVERN, IDENTIFY, PROTECT, DETECT, RESPOND, and RECOVER — organize cybersecurity outcomes at their highest level.

questions.question: How does a CSF Current Profile differ from a Target Profile?
questions.answer: A Current Profile specifies the Core outcomes the organization is currently achieving or attempting to achieve and how or to what extent they are achieved. A Target Profile specifies the desired outcomes selected and prioritized for the organization's cybersecurity risk management objectives.

claims.text: A Current Profile records Core outcomes currently achieved or attempted.
A Current Profile characterizes how or to what extent each outcome is achieved.
A Target Profile records desired Core outcomes.
Target outcomes are selected and prioritized for cybersecurity risk management objectives.

evidence.section: Appendix C. Glossary — CSF Current Profile
evidence.text: A part of an Organizational Profile that specifies the Core outcomes that an organization is currently achieving (or attempting to achieve) and characterizes how or to what extent each outcome is being achieved.

evidence.section: Appendix C. Glossary — CSF Target Profile
evidence.text: A part of an Organizational Profile that specifies the desired Core outcomes that an organization has selected and prioritized for achieving its cybersecurity risk management objectives.

questions.question: What are the four CSF Tiers, from Tier 1 through Tier 4?
questions.answer: The four Tiers are Partial (Tier 1), Risk Informed (Tier 2), Repeatable (Tier 3), and Adaptive (Tier 4).

claims.text: Tier 1 is Partial.
Tier 2 is Risk Informed.
Tier 3 is Repeatable.
Tier 4 is Adaptive.

evidence.text: The Tiers, as shown in Fig. 4 and notionally illustrated in Appendix B, reflect an organization’s practices for managing cybersecurity risk as Partial (Tier 1), Risk Informed (Tier 2), Repeatable (Tier 3), and Adaptive (Tier 4).

questions.question: What is a CSF Informative Reference?
questions.answer: An Informative Reference is a mapping that indicates a relationship between the CSF Core and standards, guidelines, regulations, or other content.

claims.text: An Informative Reference is a mapping.
It indicates relationships between the Core and standards, guidelines, regulations, or other content.

evidence.section: 4. Introduction to Online Resources That Supplement the CSF
evidence.text: Informative References are mappings that indicate relationships between the Core and various standards, guidelines, regulations, and other content.

questions.question: What must organizational cybersecurity practices be, and what should they reflect?
questions.answer: The practices must be straightforward and communicated regularly. They should reflect applying risk management to changes in mission or business requirements, threats, and the overall technical landscape.

claims.text: The practices must be straightforward.
The practices must be communicated regularly.
The practices should reflect risk management applied to changes in mission or business requirements.
The practices should reflect risk management applied to threats and the overall technical landscape.

evidence.section: GOVERN — Develop and communicate organizational cybersecurity practices
evidence.text: These must be straightforward and communicated regularly. They should reflect the application of risk management to changes in mission or business requirements, threats, and overall technical landscape.

questions.question: What three backup actions does the Resource & Overview Guide recommend under PROTECT?
questions.answer: Back up data on agreed schedules or with built-in backup capabilities, keep at least one frequently backed-up data set offline against ransomware, and test that backed-up data can be restored successfully.

claims.text: Back up data on agreed schedules or use built-in backup capabilities.
Keep at least one frequently backed-up data set offline to protect it against ransomware.
Test that backed-up data can be restored successfully.

evidence.text: Back up data at agreed-upon schedules or use built-in backup capabilities; software and cloud solutions can automate this process. Keep at least one frequently backed-up set of data offline to protect it against ransomware. Test to ensure that backed-up data can be successfully restored to systems.

questions.question: What does the RESPOND guidance say to do with incident data?
questions.answer: Collect incident data and preserve its integrity and provenance.

claims.text: Incident data is collected.

The provenance of incident data is preserved.

evidence.text: Collect incident data and preserve its integrity and provenance.

questions.question: Under AC-7, what must happen when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded?
questions.answer: The system must automatically take one or more organization-selected actions: lock the account or node for a defined period or until administrator release, delay the next prompt using a defined algorithm, notify the system administrator, or take another organization-defined action.

Locking the account or node for a defined period or until administrator release is an available action.
Delaying the next logon prompt using an organization-defined algorithm is an available action.
Notifying the system administrator is an available action.
Another organization-defined action may be selected.
